lead.headline: IBM PC Turns One With the Clone Question Already in the Room
lead.summary: Thursday, August 12 marks one year since IBM announced the Personal Computer. The first-birthday story is not cake; it is compatibility. Buyers now weigh a real IBM 5150 desk against cheaper workalikes, add-in cards, DOS disks, printers, monitors, and the growing office-software shelf. IBM opened the door with a low-cost system built from a system unit, keyboard, diskette drives, monochrome display, and printer options; by this summer, the question on the sales floor is which programs and boards will behave like they belong together.

issues.editorNote: Today's issue leans toward personal computers, home computing, software people actually used, and games people could buy or talk about in 1986.
issues.morningLine: Morning Edition: five-minute skim for personal-computer people, game-shelf watchers, and anyone who still hears a modem handshake in their soul.

lead.headline: Lotus Ends VisiCalc as 1-2-3 Era Takes Hold
lead.summary: Lotus, already dominant in PC spreadsheets, discontinued VisiCalc during the week of this issue after acquiring Software Arts in 1985. The move marked a symbolic handoff from the Apple II spreadsheet age to the IBM PC business-software era.

image.alt: Period-style clipping of a 1986 IBM-compatible computer desk with spreadsheet printouts, a CRT monitor, floppies, and dot-matrix paper
image.caption: Spreadsheet software moved the business desk toward IBM-compatible PCs.

computerItems.label: Hardware
computerItems.headline: Low-Priced IBM Compatibles Crowd the PC Aisle
computerItems.summary: InfoWorld's June 9 issue covered Epson's Equity II as a low-priced IBM-compatible challenger, a sign that clone competition was pushing business buyers toward cheaper PC-standard machines.

computerItems.label: Software
computerItems.headline: Desktop Publishing Keeps the Macintosh in the Office Conversation
computerItems.summary: Aldus PageMaker, released for Macintosh in 1985, was still drawing serious trade-press attention in June 1986 as page layout became one of the Mac's clearest professional strengths.

computerItems.label: Games
computerItems.headline: Japan Gets a Harder Super Mario Sequel
computerItems.summary: Nintendo released the Japanese Super Mario Bros. 2 for the Famicom Disk System on June 3, while Enix's Dragon Quest, released May 27, was still new on Famicom shelves.

image.alt: Period-style clipping of a 1980s mall arcade with rows of arcade cabinets and players from behind
image.caption: Arcades stayed loud while new console and computer RPGs moved into bedrooms.

computerItems.label: Workstations
computerItems.headline: IBM's RT PC Puts RISC on the Business Radar
computerItems.summary: IBM's 1986 RT PC workstation brought RISC technology into IBM's product line, though early trade coverage treated it as important but not yet a sure threat to established workstation vendors.

market.headline: Markets Desk
market.summary: The Dow finished at a record close on June 6, 1986. Nasdaq also edged higher, keeping the tech-heavy index near the 400 mark.

curiosity.headline: A 1200-Baud Modem Was Fast Enough to Feel Like the Future
curiosity.summary: At 1200 bits per second, a plain page of text could arrive in seconds instead of minutes. It was still slow by modern standards, but for BBS callers it changed the rhythm from waiting to browsing.
curiosity.detail: Think of it as the difference between mailing a postcard and watching one appear line by line.
